items.title: L13: What separates a strong answer from a good one
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Many departments score each Behaviour answer on a numerical scale, often 1 to 7, with a descriptor for each score. Departments differ, so read the candidate pack for the scale actually used.

What moves an answer up the scale is rarely length. It is the quality of evidence. A good answer describes a relevant situation, a clear personal role and a sensible result. A strong answer adds four things. First, scale and complexity appropriate to the grade: more people, more risk, more competing interests. Second, judgement: you explain the options you considered and why you chose one, rather than just reporting what you did. Third, impact beyond the task: a change that lasted, a colleague who developed, or a process others adopted. Fourth, reflection: what you learned and what you changed afterwards.

The Behaviours also have grade-specific descriptors, and promotion interviews are scored against the level for the role you want. An EO example that is entirely about completing your own work will not meet a HEO descriptor, which expects you to influence or lead others. When you choose examples, compare them with the descriptor and ask whether the evidence matches the level.

A common reason for a middling score is the absence of one element, such as a measurable result, even when the rest is good. Another is an example that is real but small. If you have evidence at a higher level in a different setting, such as voluntary work or temporary promotion, it may be better to use that than a routine example from your current post.

Finally, a strong answer is easy to follow. Signpost the Situation, Action and Result, and finish with the outcome rather than trailing off.

questions.prompt: Many departments score Behaviour answers on a numerical scale. Where should you check how your own interview will be scored?

options.text: On the intranet page of your current department, since scoring is standard across government
In the general Civil Service Code, which sets one scale for every department
In the candidate pack or job advert for the specific recruitment
In the feedback you received from a different department last year

questions.hint: Scoring scales differ by department and campaign, so the pack for the role is the reliable source.

questions.prompt: A candidate gives a long answer with detailed background, a clear role and an outcome of 'it went well'. What is the most likely reason for a middling score?

options.text: The candidate used 'I' too often, which can sound self-centred
The result is not specific or measurable, so the impact is hard to judge
The background was too detailed for the panel to follow
The answer was too long, because panels penalise any answer over three minutes

questions.hint: Evidence of impact is a common gap even in otherwise good answers.

questions.prompt: Which addition most clearly lifts an answer from good to strong?

options.text: A longer description of the situation so the panel has full context
An explanation of the options you weighed and why you chose one
A statement that your manager was pleased with the work
A second example that confirms the first one

questions.hint: Judgement is shown by the reasoning behind a choice, not just the action taken.

questions.prompt: An EO describes finishing a large batch of casework on time, all by themselves, for a HEO interview. What is the main shortfall?

options.text: The example is too small, because HEO examples must involve a budget of some size and several teams
The example uses casework, which panels do not accept as evidence at HEO because it is operational work
The example has no stated result, since meeting a deadline is an output and not an outcome
The example shows personal delivery, whereas the HEO level expects influence over others

questions.hint: HEO descriptors usually expect leading or influencing others, not only personal output.

questions.prompt: Why compare a draft example with the descriptor for the grade you want?

options.text: It tells you which exact words the panel will be listening for and how to include them in your answer
It allows you to copy the descriptor wording into your answer, so that the panel can tick it off
It confirms whether the example is recent enough to be accepted under the department's rules
It shows whether the evidence matches the level of scale, complexity and influence expected

questions.hint: Descriptors define what is expected at each grade.

questions.prompt: You have a routine example from your current role and a stronger one from voluntary work. What is the best choice?

options.text: Use the work example, because panels discount anything that comes from outside the Civil Service
Use whichever gives the more convincing evidence at the grade, and say clearly where it comes from
Combine both into one answer, so that the panel sees a wider range of experience in a single story
Use the voluntary example only if the panel asks about outside experience at the end

questions.hint: The relevance of the evidence matters more than the setting.

questions.prompt: Which closing sentence best finishes a strong answer?

options.text: I hope that gives you a clear picture of what I did, and I would be glad to expand on any part
As a result, error rates halved within a quarter and the team kept the new process in place after I moved on
That is really all I can think of on that question, though there may be other examples I could give
So overall I think it was a successful project and I learned a great deal from being involved in it

questions.hint: It ends on a concrete, lasting result rather than trailing off.

questions.prompt: What does 'impact beyond the task' mean in a strong answer?

options.text: A change that lasted, such as a process others adopted or a colleague who developed
A task that took longer than planned but was completed to the standard that the manager had asked for
A task whose result was recognised in a team newsletter or by a senior leader in a public message
A task that involved more than one department, which means that the result has a wider audience

questions.hint: It shows lasting effect rather than a one-off output.

questions.prompt: Why is length rarely what lifts a score?

options.text: Panels are told to prefer short answers because they have a long list of candidates to see in a day
Panels stop listening after two minutes whatever you say, so only the opening part of an answer is scored
Panels score the quality and relevance of evidence, not the number of words
Longer answers are more likely to contain errors, which the panel then counts against the candidate

questions.hint: A well-evidenced concise answer can score higher than a long one that lacks a result.

questions.prompt: How should you signpost an answer so that a panel can follow it?

options.text: Describe the situation in detail and leave the panel to infer your actions from what happened next
Tell the story in strict date order from the first email to the last, so that nothing is missed
Start with the result and then explain how you reached it, leaving out the situation to save time
Make the Situation, your Actions and the Result clear, and end on the outcome

questions.hint: A clear structure helps the panel find and score the evidence.

items.title: L13: Presentations that make a case: the so-what, evidence and call to action
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing (GOV.UK)
items.body:
A competent presentation informs. A strong one makes a case. At HEO and SEO level, the panel wants to see you move an audience to a decision or a changed view, so the structure should be built around an argument rather than a tour of the facts.

A useful pattern has three moves. First, the headline: say in one sentence what you want the audience to believe or do. Second, the reasons: usually two or three, each supported by a piece of evidence such as a figure, a comparison or an example. Third, the call to action: what happens next, who does it and by when. If you cannot state your headline in a single sentence, the argument is not yet clear.

For each point, test it with the question 'so what?' A statement that three regions missed their targets means little until you say why it matters, such as that it puts the annual target at risk. Panels listen for implications, not only information.

Use data sparingly. One chart with a clear title that states its message, such as 'Waiting times have doubled in a year', does more than a table of fifty figures. Round numbers where precision adds nothing, and give the source of any figure you rely on.

Pre-empt the likely objections. Naming the strongest counter-argument and answering it shows judgement and builds trust. If something has gone wrong in the middle of the talk, such as a lost slide or a wrong figure, correct it simply and carry on; a calm correction is often noticed more favourably than an attempt to hide it.

Finish by repeating your headline and the next step, then stop. Do not end with a tail of apologies or a hopeful 'any questions?' without a final message.

questions.prompt: What should a presentation built as an argument start with?

options.text: A short history of the issue so the audience shares your starting point
One sentence saying what you want the audience to believe or do
A list of everything you intend to cover, in the order you will cover it
An outline of the data sources you have drawn on

questions.hint: A clear headline sets the direction for everything else.

questions.prompt: What does the test 'so what?' ask you to do for each point?

options.text: Add another statistic that supports the point
Shorten the point so that it fits on one slide
Check that the point is not repeated elsewhere
Say why it matters and what follows from it

questions.hint: Panels listen for implications, not only information.

questions.prompt: A slide shows three regions missed their targets. Which version has a stronger 'so what'?

options.text: Three regions missed their targets, which puts the annual target at risk
Targets were missed in the north, the east and the south west, with the south west furthest behind
The regions whose targets were missed are shown in red on the dashboard on the next slide
Three of the nine regions missed their targets this quarter, according to the latest management figures

questions.hint: It states the implication rather than only the fact.

questions.prompt: Which chart title is most effective in a presentation to a senior audience?

options.text: Chart showing waiting time data
Waiting times by month, April to March
Waiting times have doubled in a year
Figure 3: Waiting times

questions.hint: A title that states the message tells the audience what to take from the chart.

questions.prompt: The audience is likely to raise a strong objection to your recommendation. What is the best approach?

options.text: Cover it on a back-up slide that you do not present unless the panel asks you about it directly
Name the strongest objection yourself and answer it as part of the presentation
Leave it out and answer it only if somebody raises it, so that your time goes on your own message
Mention it in the final minute so that there is little time left for the audience to discuss it

questions.hint: Pre-empting objections shows judgement and builds trust.

questions.prompt: You realise a figure on your slide is wrong in the middle of your presentation. What is the best response?

options.text: Stop the presentation and restart with a corrected version
Apologise at length and ask the panel whether they wish you to continue
Ignore it and hope that nobody notices before you finish
Correct it simply, give the right figure and carry on

questions.hint: A calm correction protects credibility.

questions.prompt: How should numbers be used on slides for a senior audience?

options.text: As a table of all the available figures, so that nobody can say that relevant data was held back
Sparingly, rounded where precision adds nothing, with the source named for key figures
Only in the speaker's notes, with none of them on the slides, so that the audience listens to you
In full detail, so that the audience can check every calculation and see that nothing has been left out

questions.hint: Clear, limited data supports the message.

questions.prompt: What should the call to action include?

options.text: A summary of the options that you did not choose
What happens next, who does it and by when
A promise to return with further analysis if needed
A request that the audience reads your supporting paper

questions.hint: A concrete next step turns persuasion into a decision.

questions.prompt: Which closing is strongest for a presentation?

options.text: Summarise every point in the order that you made it
Thank the panel for their time and say you hope it was helpful
Ask the panel which part they would like you to cover again
Repeat the headline and the next step, then stop

questions.hint: A final restatement leaves the key message and action in the audience's minds.

questions.prompt: If you cannot state the headline of a presentation in one sentence, what does that tell you?

options.text: The audience is likely to disagree with you, so you should prepare the evidence more carefully
The argument is not yet clear enough to present
The slides need to be redesigned so that the message is easier to see at a glance
The topic is too broad for the time allowed, so you should narrow the subject before you begin

questions.hint: Clarity of the central claim comes before design.

items.title: L13: Written submissions for senior readers
items.source: Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance and Civil Service Code (GOV.UK)
items.body:
A submission is a formal piece of written advice to a senior person, often a minister or director, asking them to take a decision or note a position. At HEO and SEO level you may be asked to write a short one in an exercise. You do not need to know the department's format; you need to show the habits that make advice useful.

A typical structure starts with a purpose line stating what is being asked: 'You are asked to agree option 2.' Then comes a short summary giving the recommendation and the main reasons. After that come the background, the options with their costs, benefits and risks, the recommendation again in more detail, and the next steps, with any handling points such as who else has been consulted and whether the matter is sensitive. Long supporting detail goes into annexes, so that the main text stays short.

The Civil Service Code requires that advice is honest and objective. In practice this means setting out facts accurately, giving a balanced account of the options even where you recommend one, and not hiding inconvenient evidence or risks to make a recommendation more attractive. Officials give advice; ministers decide. Once a decision is taken, officials carry it out, provided it is lawful.

Write for a reader with little time and no knowledge of the detail. Use short paragraphs, plain words, and define any abbreviation on first use. Put the answer first.

Finally, keep tone neutral. A submission is not a campaign document.

questions.prompt: What is a submission in the Civil Service?

options.text: Formal written advice asking a senior person to take a decision or note a position
A public statement that sets out the department's policy on a matter for the benefit of citizens
A summary of a meeting that is sent to attendees afterwards, recording what was decided and by whom
A written reply to a member of the public who has complained about a service the department runs

questions.hint: It is advice to a decision-maker.

questions.prompt: Which line best opens a submission?

options.text: Please find attached the detailed analysis of the options, which has been prepared with finance colleagues
This submission provides some background on the project and on the choices that have arisen so far
I am writing to set out a number of issues that you may wish to consider in the coming weeks
You are asked to agree option 2, which is recommended for the reasons below

questions.hint: A clear ask at the start orients the reader.

questions.prompt: Where should long supporting detail go?

options.text: In footnotes at the end of each paragraph
In a separate email sent after the submission
In annexes, so the main text stays short
In the first paragraph, so the reader sees all the evidence first

questions.hint: Annexes allow detail without lengthening the main advice.

questions.prompt: Which Civil Service Code principle most directly requires advice to set out inconvenient evidence?

options.text: Impartiality, which requires officials to act equally for governments of any party
Objectivity, which requires advice based on the evidence and a fair account of the options
Honesty, which requires officials to be truthful about what they themselves have done
Integrity, which requires officials to place public interest above their personal interests

questions.hint: Objectivity requires decisions and advice to be based on rigorous analysis of the evidence.

questions.prompt: An official recommends option 2 but knows its main risk is serious. What should the submission do?

options.text: State the risk clearly alongside the recommendation and say how it could be managed
Leave the risk out, since the minister is likely to have been told about it through another route
Present the risk as unlikely, so that the recommendation remains persuasive for the decision-maker
Mention the risk briefly in an annex so that the main text stays positive and easy for the reader

questions.hint: Honest advice includes the risks that matter.

questions.prompt: Finance and legal colleagues disagree with your recommendation. How should the submission report this?

options.text: Set out their views fairly so the decision-maker can weigh them
Mention that there were comments, without giving their substance
Report them only if the decision-maker asks
Leave their views out, because you have the final say on advice

questions.hint: Fair reporting of consultation is part of honest advice.

questions.prompt: After a minister takes a lawful decision against your advice, what do officials do?

options.text: Carry it out, having given their advice
Delay action until the next submission
Ask the minister to reconsider until they agree
Pass the decision to another official

questions.hint: Officials advise and ministers decide.

questions.prompt: Why should a submission use short paragraphs and plain words?

options.text: Panels in exercises mark long paragraphs down, whatever the subject and whatever the audience is
Plain words make a submission look more senior, which helps persuade the reader to agree
Short paragraphs allow the reader to skim the headings only, which is why the detail can be left out
The reader has little time and may not know the detail

questions.hint: Clarity serves a busy reader.

questions.prompt: A submission mentions a figure of 12 per cent in the summary and 15 per cent in the detail. What is the problem?

options.text: The inconsistency undermines credibility and may mislead the reader
It is acceptable, since summaries are only ever approximate and the detail is what counts for decisions
Only the summary figure matters, because the detail is for officials rather than for the decision-maker
The detail should be removed, because only the summary is read by a senior reader

questions.hint: Numbers must agree throughout.

questions.prompt: Which tone is appropriate for a submission?

options.text: Forceful, to secure agreement
Neutral and professional, setting out advice
Cautious and hedged, to avoid being blamed
Enthusiastic, to show commitment to the policy

questions.hint: A submission advises rather than campaigns.

items.title: L13: Bias and fairness: what panels guard against
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles; Equality Act 2010 guidance (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Panels are trained to avoid several well-known biases, and understanding them helps you make your evidence stand out. Knowing the names also helps you recognise them in practice.

The halo effect occurs when one impressive quality, such as a polished opening, colours a panellist's view of everything else. The horns effect is the reverse: one weak answer drags down later scores. Similar-to-me bias favours candidates who share a panellist's background, school or manner. First-impression bias gives too much weight to the opening minutes. The contrast effect means a candidate may be scored higher or lower because of the one before. Confirmation bias means looking for evidence that supports an early judgement.

Panels reduce these risks through structure. They use the same questions for every candidate, take notes of the evidence, score each answer separately against descriptors, score before discussing, and moderate differences by reference to the evidence. Some panels include a member from outside the team, and panellists are expected to declare any connection to a candidate.

For candidates, the lesson is practical. Treat each question as a fresh start, because answers are scored separately and a poor answer need not harm the next. Give clear, specific evidence so that any score can be justified from the notes. Do not assume a panellist shares your background: explain context and acronyms.

The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination because of protected characteristics, including age, disability, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. Employers must make reasonable adjustments for disabled applicants. Panels should not ask about these characteristics except where adjustments or monitoring are concerned, and equality monitoring information is usually kept apart from the selection decision.

If you think the process has been unfair, raise it with the recruitment contact or follow the department's complaint route.

questions.prompt: A panellist is impressed by a candidate's confident opening and rates the later answers higher than the evidence warrants. Which bias is this?

options.text: The halo effect
The horns effect
Contrast effect from the previous candidate
Confirmation bias against the candidate

questions.hint: One strong quality colours the view of everything else.

questions.prompt: Which bias is described by one weak answer lowering the scores for later answers?

options.text: The halo effect
First-impression bias
Similar-to-me bias
The horns effect

questions.hint: It is the reverse of the halo effect.

questions.prompt: A panellist favours a candidate who attended the same university. Which bias is this?

options.text: The halo effect, because one shared quality is allowed to colour the whole assessment
Similar-to-me bias
Contrast effect, because the candidate is being compared with the one who was interviewed before
Confirmation bias, because the panellist looks for evidence that fits a view already formed

questions.hint: Favouring people who are like us is a well-known bias.

questions.prompt: What is the main way structured interviews reduce bias?

options.text: Keeping the panel's notes confidential from each other until the candidate has left the building
Allowing each panellist to ask whatever they think is most relevant, so that every candidate is tested fully
Letting the chair decide each score alone, so that there is one consistent standard through the day
Asking the same questions and scoring each answer against descriptors, with notes

questions.hint: Structure and evidence make scoring consistent.

questions.prompt: Why do panellists usually score before discussing their views?

options.text: So that candidates can be told their scores sooner, which is part of fair treatment under the principles
So that one person's opinion does not sway the others
So that the chair has less to do afterwards, as most of the decisions have already been made
So that panel notes can be shorter, as the panel has already agreed on the main points before writing

questions.hint: Independent scoring limits influence.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate respond after giving what they think was a poor answer?

options.text: Treat the next question as a fresh start, since answers are scored separately
Apologise briefly to the panel and then carry on, so that they know that you recognise the poor answer
Ask to return to the earlier question at the end of the interview and give a better answer
Try to make up for it by giving a much longer answer to the next question, so the overall score recovers

questions.hint: Separate scoring means a poor answer need not harm later ones.

questions.prompt: Which characteristic is protected under the Equality Act 2010?

options.text: Length of service
Disability
Educational background
Place of work

questions.hint: Disability is among the protected characteristics.

questions.prompt: What must employers do for a disabled applicant who needs help to take part fairly?

options.text: Offer a different job at a lower grade
Allow the applicant to skip some questions
Make reasonable adjustments
Reduce the pass mark for the applicant

questions.hint: Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty.

questions.prompt: Equality monitoring information collected at application stage is usually

options.text: shared with the panel to help with scoring
used to set the pass mark for each group
reported to the candidate with the result
kept apart from the selection decision

questions.hint: Monitoring is separate from selection.

questions.prompt: Which action is correct if you believe the process has been unfair?

options.text: Post a comment on social media so that the department sees how the process looked from the outside
Raise it with the recruitment contact or follow the department's complaint route
Withdraw your application without comment, so as not to damage your chances in later competitions
Tell the panel at the end of the interview that you think the process was unfair, so that they can respond

questions.hint: Formal routes exist for raising concerns.

items.title: L13: Strengths and Behaviours in a combined interview
items.body:
Some promotion interviews combine Behaviours and Strengths questions, and may add a short Experience or Technical element. Each tests something different, and switching between them takes care.

Behaviours questions ask what you did in a particular past situation. They reward evidence: a specific example, your own actions and a result. Strengths questions ask about what you enjoy and do naturally, often in short, quick-fire form. They reward energy, honesty and a sense that the answer is your own. If you answer a strengths question with a long, structured story, you will take time from later questions and sound rehearsed. If you answer a Behaviour question with a general statement of preference, you will leave the panel with no evidence.

The panel often signals the change of mode by announcing it: 'We are now moving to the strengths section.' If the signal is missing, listen to the wording. 'Tell us about a time when' invites a STAR example; 'What do you enjoy about' or 'What is your preferred way to' invites a short, natural answer.

Plan your examples so that they do not duplicate across Behaviours. A strong example can sometimes cover two Behaviours, but the panel will mark each answer separately, so avoid repeating the same story unless you emphasise a different aspect.

Strengths and Behaviours can also support each other. If you say you love developing others, your Behaviour example for Developing Self and Others should match it. Panels will notice inconsistency between the two halves.

If Experience or Technical elements are included, expect questions on your career or specific skills. Keep these factual and brief, and link them to the role. Throughout, pace your energy so that your final answers are as good as your first.

questions.prompt: Which question invites a STAR-style example?

options.text: Which part of your current role gives you the most energy in a typical working week?
Tell us about a time when you led a team through a difficult period
What is your preferred way to start a new piece of work when the brief is unclear?
What do you enjoy most about managing people and getting the best from them?

questions.hint: 'Tell us about a time when' asks for a specific past event.

questions.prompt: A candidate answers a quick-fire strengths question with a three-minute STAR story. What is the likely effect?

options.text: The panel gives extra credit for the evidence, since a full example always scores higher than a short one
The answer is scored under the wrong Behaviour, because strengths and Behaviours share a scale
There is no effect, because time limits in strengths sections are flexible and decided by the panel
Time is taken from later questions and the answer may sound rehearsed

questions.hint: Strengths questions suit short, natural answers.

questions.prompt: Why is a general statement of preference a weak answer to a Behaviour question?

options.text: It is too short to be heard
It shows you did not understand the strengths framework
It makes the panel suspicious of your honesty
It gives the panel no specific evidence to score

questions.hint: Behaviours need past evidence.

questions.prompt: If the panel does not announce a change of section, how can you tell which type of question is being asked?

options.text: Wait for the chair to tell you how to answer, and do not speak until they have done so
Listen to the wording, such as 'tell us about a time' or 'what do you enjoy'
Watch whether the panel member is holding a sheet of paper or reading from the screen
Assume that it is a Behaviours question until the panel tells you that it is not

questions.hint: Wording usually signals the type.

questions.prompt: How should you treat the same example when two Behaviours both seem to call for it?

options.text: Reuse it if you must, but emphasise a different aspect for each Behaviour
Reuse it freely and tell the panel in advance, so that they know the repetition is deliberate
Reuse it only if the two Behaviours are in the same group, since other pairings test different things
Never reuse it, because panels reject repeated examples outright and may score both answers down

questions.hint: Reusing needs different emphasis.

questions.prompt: You say you love developing others. What should your Developing Self and Others example show?

options.text: A different example in which you developed yourself
Concrete evidence consistent with that enjoyment
A general account of what training you offer
An example about how you manage performance

questions.hint: Panels notice inconsistency between sections.

questions.prompt: When the interview includes Experience questions, what is the best approach?

options.text: Keep answers factual and brief and link them to the role
Use the questions to repeat your Behaviour examples at greater length, as they carry the most weight
Give a full account of your whole career from your first job, so that the panel has the complete picture
Say that the application form already covers it and invite the panel to refer to it instead

questions.hint: Experience questions are factual.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to pace your energy through a long interview?

options.text: The panel will decide after the first few answers, so energy at the start matters most of all
Candidates who finish early are scored higher, because the panel regards brevity as good judgement
The panel gives more weight to the last questions, as they are the ones remembered at the scoring stage
Late answers are scored too, and energy is part of strengths scoring

questions.hint: Every answer counts.

questions.prompt: Which phrase marks a strengths question?

options.text: Tell us about a decision you regret
What do you find most satisfying at work?
Describe a time when you handled a conflict
Give an example of working to a tight deadline

questions.hint: It asks about preference, not a past event.

questions.prompt: What is the best preparation for a combined interview?

options.text: Prepare Behaviour examples and reflect on strengths, keeping both consistent
Learn answers by heart for both types, so that nothing depends on thinking on your feet
Prepare only Behaviour examples and improvise the strengths, since they are meant to be spontaneous
Prepare strengths answers only, since strengths questions usually carry the greater weight in scoring

questions.hint: Both need different preparation.

items.title: L13: Leading inclusively and leading without authority
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Leadership and Working Together; Civil Service People Plan (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Leadership questions at HEO and SEO increasingly ask about inclusion and influence. Two themes recur: how you lead a team whose members differ in background, working pattern and need, and how you lead when you have no formal authority over the people you need.

Inclusive leadership means making sure every member of the team can contribute and develop. Practical behaviours include inviting quieter colleagues to speak in meetings, rotating who chairs or presents, checking that opportunities such as stretch work are offered fairly rather than to the same people, and being thoughtful about hybrid and part-time arrangements so that those who are not in the office are not left out. Employees have a statutory right to request flexible working, and a good manager considers requests on their merits and in line with the department's policy. Reasonable adjustments for disabled colleagues are a legal duty, and a leader who arranges them promptly and without making a fuss shows good practice.

Leading without authority is common in the Civil Service because delivery often depends on other teams, other departments and external partners. Effective approaches include understanding what the other party needs, finding common goals, building trust through reliability, being clear about what you are asking and why, and using evidence rather than pressure. When you need to escalate, do it openly, after giving the person a chance to resolve the issue, and in terms of the shared objective.

In interviews, panels look for specific acts: what you changed, how you found out what people needed and how you checked it worked. Avoid generalities such as 'I treat everyone the same'. Treating people fairly sometimes means treating them differently, according to their needs, and that is worth saying.

questions.prompt: Which action is an example of inclusive leadership in team meetings?

options.text: Asking the team to send written comments only, so that nobody dominates the discussion
Giving the most experienced person the final say on every item so that discussion stays efficient
Inviting quieter colleagues to contribute and rotating who presents
Holding meetings only at times that suit the full-time staff, so that attendance stays high

questions.hint: It gives everyone a chance to contribute.

questions.prompt: Stretch opportunities keep going to the same two people. What is the best response?

options.text: Check how opportunities are offered and make sure they are shared fairly
Carry on as you are, because the two people involved have the most experience and will deliver best
Hand the work out at random whatever people's skills, so that nobody can claim favouritism
Ask for volunteers and give the work to whoever replies first, so that the process is open to all

questions.hint: Fair offer of opportunity is part of inclusive leadership.

questions.prompt: How should a manager treat a request to work flexibly?

options.text: Refuse it unless the employee has a medical reason, since the needs of the service come first
Defer it until the end of the reporting year so that every request can be compared fairly
Consider it on its merits and in line with the department's policy
Accept it automatically, because the right to request flexible working is also a right to have it

questions.hint: Employees have a statutory right to request, not to have it granted automatically.

questions.prompt: A disabled colleague needs adjustments. Which approach shows good practice?

options.text: Offer a different role, so that adjustments are not needed and the team's work stays unchanged
Wait until the colleague has asked more than once, so that you know the need is a genuine one
Ask HR to decide whether the colleague is truly disabled before any change is made to their work
Arrange them promptly and without making it a problem for the colleague

questions.hint: Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty.

questions.prompt: What does leading without authority mean?

options.text: Leading in a way that avoids making decisions yourself, so that the team takes ownership
Taking charge of a project in an emergency before senior managers have had time to appoint a lead
Getting results from people who do not report to you
Leading a team after your own manager has left and nobody has yet been appointed in their place

questions.hint: It describes influence across boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour best helps when you need another team to deliver something for you?

options.text: Setting a firm deadline and copying their manager in, so that there is a clear record of the ask
Pointing out that your request has the backing of a senior sponsor, so that it is treated as a priority
Understanding what that team needs and linking your request to a shared goal
Offering to take over the work yourself, so that you stay in control of the quality and timing

questions.hint: Influence rests on shared goals and trust.

questions.prompt: When must escalation be considered?

options.text: Never, because going over someone's head always damages the relationship beyond repair
As soon as there is any delay, so that the senior people can see problems before they grow
Only when a senior person asks you to, since escalating on your own initiative looks like blame
When the person has had a chance to resolve the issue and the shared objective is at risk

questions.hint: Escalation should be open and a last step.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I treat everyone the same' a weak answer?

options.text: It sounds defensive, because a manager confident of fair treatment would give a detailed account
Panels always prefer a longer answer, and this one is too short to evidence anything
It suggests that you do not value diversity, and the panel will mark you down for it
It does not show what you did, and fairness sometimes means treating people differently according to need

questions.hint: Specific actions matter.

questions.prompt: Which description of a mistake shows learning in an inclusion example?

options.text: I did not realise anyone minded the meeting times until HR raised it, and I left them as they were
I moved the meetings online, which solved the problem for the part-time staff and for everyone else
I scheduled meetings when part-time colleagues were not working; I now agree times with the whole team
I changed the meeting time after the first complaint and have not heard anything further since

questions.hint: Specific, owned learning.

questions.prompt: How can you check that an inclusion change has worked?

options.text: Look at attendance figures, which show whether the new arrangements are suiting people
Ask the team and look at who is contributing and taking up opportunities
Wait for the next staff survey, which is the proper way to measure inclusion in a department
Ask your own manager, since they can tell whether the team's way of working has improved

questions.hint: Evidence from people and participation.

items.title: L13: Managing performance, attendance and adjustments fairly
items.source: ACAS guidance on discipline, absence and reasonable adjustments; Equality Act 2010 (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Interview questions on managing underperformance and absence test whether you balance firmness with fairness and know when to seek advice. 

When performance is below standard, a manager first tries to understand why. Causes can include unclear expectations, lack of training, workload, health, or personal difficulties. A fair approach sets clear and measurable expectations, offers support, agrees a review date and keeps a record. Informal action comes before formal capability procedures where it is appropriate. Throughout, the manager takes advice from HR, who help to make sure the process is lawful and consistent.

Where health may be involved, the Equality Act 2010 matters. A disabled employee is protected from discrimination and entitled to reasonable adjustments, such as changed hours, equipment or a revised task allocation. A manager does not have to make a medical diagnosis; if an employee mentions a health condition, the manager should ask what would help and involve occupational health and HR as the policy requires.

For sickness absence, good practice includes keeping in touch in a way that is supportive, holding a return-to-work conversation, and looking at patterns of absence only with the right advice and records. A manager should not press for details of a condition, and personal health information is sensitive and confidential.

In an interview, describe what you did and avoid detail that could identify the person. Show that you were consistent, that you documented key conversations and that you treated the person with respect while still addressing the standard. It is worth saying what you learned, such as that earlier intervention would have saved months of difficulty.

Avoid answers that suggest you went straight to formal action or, at the other extreme, that you let problems drift.

questions.prompt: What should a manager try to establish first when performance is below standard?

options.text: How the person compares with colleagues who do similar work, so the standard is set fairly
Whether the person wants to stay in the team, since that affects how much support is worthwhile
Why it is happening, such as unclear expectations, training gaps, workload or health
Whether a formal warning is likely to be needed, so that you can plan the stages of the process

questions.hint: Understanding causes comes first.

questions.prompt: Which combination reflects a fair approach to underperformance?

options.text: Clear measurable expectations, support, a review date and a written record
A team discussion about standards in general, so that the individual is not singled out
A written warning followed by a deadline, so that the person understands that their job is at risk
A change of tasks without explanation, so that the person is not embarrassed by a formal discussion

questions.hint: Fair processes are specific and supported.

questions.prompt: Why does a manager take advice from HR during a performance process?

options.text: To speed up the process, because HR can approve the formal stage without needing evidence
To pass responsibility for the decision to HR, so that the manager is not blamed if it is challenged
To help ensure the process is lawful and consistent
To avoid having to talk to the employee directly, since HR can manage the whole conversation

questions.hint: HR support legal and consistent handling.

questions.prompt: An employee mentions a health condition that affects their work. What should the manager do?

options.text: Ask what would help and involve occupational health and HR as the policy requires
Ask for the diagnosis in writing before any change, so that the department has the facts on file
Reduce the person's workload without discussion, so that the pressure on them eases at once
Wait until the employee provides formal evidence, since managers must not act on a verbal mention

questions.hint: A manager need not diagnose; they ask what would help.

questions.prompt: Which of these may be a reasonable adjustment?

options.text: A permanent change of grade to a role with fewer demands, whatever the employee's own view
Removal of all targets for the employee, so that their work is not measured against the team
A pay rise to compensate the employee for the extra effort that their condition requires
Changed hours or specialist equipment

questions.hint: Adjustments remove disadvantage in the workplace.

questions.prompt: After a period of sickness absence, which step is good practice?

options.text: Immediate formal review of attendance
Asking for full details of the diagnosis
Extra work to make up lost time
A supportive return-to-work conversation

questions.hint: Supportive and proportionate.

questions.prompt: Why should a manager not press for details of a condition?

options.text: The manager can find the details on the personnel file, so there is no need to ask
Health information is sensitive and the employee need only share what helps with support
Employees have no duty to attend occupational health, so the manager cannot ask for details
It is against the law for a manager to ask about health at all, whatever the circumstances

questions.hint: Confidentiality and respect.

questions.prompt: Which interview answer shows weak judgement?

options.text: I kept notes of the meetings and asked the person to confirm them afterwards
I went straight to the formal procedure without discussing it with the person
I agreed expectations and a review date with the person and followed up in writing
I took advice from HR before the first meeting and kept to the department's procedure

questions.hint: Informal steps should usually come first.

questions.prompt: Which interview answer shows weak judgement at the opposite extreme?

options.text: I involved occupational health once the person mentioned that the problem might be linked to health
I agreed a plan with the person and checked back on progress at each of the agreed review points
I hoped the problem would resolve on its own, so I raised it only after a year
I raised it early and gave the person clear support, with a date on which to review progress

questions.hint: Drift makes problems worse.

questions.prompt: What is a sound lesson to draw from a performance example?

options.text: Standards should be lowered where a person has health difficulties, so that nobody is disadvantaged
Formal action should be quicker, because informal steps only delay a decision that is inevitable
Colleagues should be told about the case, so that the standard is understood across the team
Earlier intervention would have saved months of difficulty

questions.hint: Learning shows reflection.

items.title: L13: Making your own role clear in complex programmes
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours; Government Functional Standard for project delivery (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Complex programmes involve many people, and attributing results to individuals is hard. Panels know this, but they still need to score you on what you did. The skill is to describe your role in a way that is precise, honest and shows scale.

Start with where you sat in the work. State your role, who you reported to and who reported to you, and what you were accountable for. In project language, someone who is accountable owns the outcome, someone who is responsible does the work, others are consulted and others are informed. If you were accountable for a workstream rather than the whole programme, say so. Naming the boundary helps the panel judge scale.

Then describe decisions that were yours. In large programmes, decisions are often shared or escalated, so identify those you took or recommended and the reasoning. For example: 'I decided to phase the roll-out by region, based on the risk analysis I prepared, and my director approved it.' This shows both ownership and a realistic chain of approval.

Where your influence was indirect, show how you used it: briefing a board, brokering a compromise between teams or challenging an assumption in a review. Influence is evidence of leadership, provided you can describe the effect it had.

Benefits should be treated with care. A programme may claim a saving, but you should say only what you can support and how it was measured. If the benefit was realised after you left, say so, and describe the part you played in setting it up.

If a panel asks 'What would have happened without you?', give an honest, specific answer, such as that the roll-out would have started in all regions at once. Avoid saying everything would have failed, which sounds like overclaiming.

questions.prompt: Why is describing where you sat in a programme a good starting point?

options.text: It sets the boundaries of your accountability so the panel can judge scale
It shows that you understand the structure chart and where each senior person sits within it
It allows you to avoid talking about your own actions until the panel presses you for them
It gives the panel names to check with, so that they can confirm your account with colleagues

questions.hint: Role and boundaries frame the evidence.

questions.prompt: In project terms, who is accountable for an outcome?

options.text: The person who does most of the day-to-day work needed to deliver the outcome
The person who must be kept informed about progress, so that they can respond when asked
The person who owns it and answers for it
The person who is consulted first on the main decisions and whose agreement is required

questions.hint: Accountability is ownership of the outcome.

questions.prompt: You were accountable for one workstream in a large programme. How should you describe this?

options.text: Describe the whole programme as yours, to show the largest possible scale of responsibility
Avoid mentioning the structure so the panel is not distracted from the outcomes you achieved
State that your accountability covered that workstream and describe the scale of it
Describe the programme as a team effort led by your director, with you as one of the team

questions.hint: Naming the boundary helps panels judge scale honestly.

questions.prompt: Which statement shows both ownership and a realistic approval chain?

options.text: I led the roll-out and took all of the decisions about how it would proceed across the regions
The roll-out was phased by region, as the board agreed after considering the risk papers
I helped to plan the roll-out with the rest of the team, and we agreed the phasing together
I decided to phase the roll-out by region, based on my risk analysis, and my director approved it

questions.hint: It shows your decision and who approved it.

questions.prompt: How can indirect influence be shown as evidence?

options.text: State that you had good relationships with senior people, and that they listened to you
Describe how you used it, such as brokering a compromise, and the effect it had
List the meetings you attended to show how widely you were engaged across the programme
Describe how much time you spent on influencing, to show how much effort it took

questions.hint: Evidence needs the action and the effect.

questions.prompt: A programme claimed a saving. What should you do when describing it?

options.text: Estimate a larger figure that reflects the whole programme, since your own part cannot be isolated
Say only what you can support and how it was measured
Avoid mentioning the saving, since a figure can be challenged and a general benefit cannot
Quote the programme's headline saving as your own, since you were part of the programme

questions.hint: Benefits claims must be supportable.

questions.prompt: A benefit was realised after you left. How should you handle this honestly?

options.text: Say so and describe the part you played in setting it up
Claim it as your result, since the groundwork you did made the later benefit possible
Say that it was not your responsibility, so that the panel does not credit you for work you did not do
Leave it out of the answer, because the panel only scores benefits you saw while you were there

questions.hint: Honest attribution.

questions.prompt: Asked, 'What would have happened without you?', which answer is best?

options.text: Nothing would have been different, because someone else on the team would have done the same
The roll-out would probably have started in all regions at once, with higher risk
Nothing could be said, because a counterfactual cannot be known and the panel should not ask it
The whole programme would have failed, because my analysis was the only thing holding it together

questions.hint: Specific and realistic.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is a sign of overclaiming?

options.text: I escalated the risk to the board when it became clear that the timetable was unrealistic
I prepared the analysis that the board used to make the decision on phasing
Without me, the programme would have collapsed
My part was the regional phasing, which my director signed off after reviewing the evidence

questions.hint: It is exaggerated.

questions.prompt: Why do panels ask who reported to you and who you reported to?

options.text: It helps them judge the scale and level of your responsibility
It is a standard question that is asked in every interview and carries no marks
They want to know whether the team liked you, since that shows how you handle people
They want to check your references, and the line manager is the first person that they contact

questions.hint: Scale and level.

items.title: L13: Case studies with trade-offs and reversible decisions
items.source: HM Treasury Green Book and Civil Service Success Profiles: Making Effective Decisions (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Strong case-study answers at HEO and SEO level go beyond listing options. They deal openly with trade-offs, uncertainty and the difference between decisions that can be reversed and those that cannot.

A trade-off arises when you cannot have everything: faster delivery may cost more, wider coverage may reduce quality, and protecting one group may delay another. Say which criteria matter most and why, and make the weighting explicit. If the case says the objective is to help the most disadvantaged users first, that should shape your choice even if another option is cheaper.

Uncertainty is normal. The Green Book encourages testing how sensitive the answer is to the main assumptions: if costs rise by a fifth or demand is lower than expected, does the preferred option still win? Saying 'my recommendation holds unless demand falls below X' is far stronger than presenting a single number as certain.

Distinguish reversible from irreversible decisions. Where a step can be undone cheaply, such as a small pilot, it is reasonable to act on imperfect information and learn. Where it cannot, such as closing a service or signing a long contract, more evidence and wider consultation are justified. A common approach is to take no-regrets actions now, which are worth doing in every scenario, and to defer irreversible ones until a trigger point is reached.

Think also about proportionality and fairness. Check who benefits and who loses, including people with protected characteristics, and note where an equality impact assessment would be needed.

Finally, say how you would know if the decision were going wrong. Name measures, a review date and what would make you change course. A recommendation with a monitoring plan shows you manage decisions, not only make them.

questions.prompt: What is a trade-off in a case study?

options.text: A decision that is shared with another team, so that responsibility is divided between the two
A compromise reached after consultation, in which every stakeholder agrees to give something up
A situation where improving one thing means accepting a cost in another
A choice between two options that are equally good, so that either could be justified

questions.hint: Trade-offs require choices between criteria.

questions.prompt: The case says the objective is to help the most disadvantaged users first. What follows?

options.text: Cost should be the deciding factor, because public money is limited and must be spent carefully
That objective should shape the weighting of criteria, even if another option is cheaper
The senior stakeholder's preferred option should be chosen, because they carry the accountability
The option that helps most users overall should win, because it gives the greatest total benefit

questions.hint: Objectives determine weighting.

questions.prompt: What does a sensitivity test ask?

options.text: Whether the preferred option still wins if key assumptions change
Whether the options have been described fairly, without any bias in favour of the preferred one
Whether stakeholders are sensitive to the change and likely to resist it when it is announced
Whether the costs are accurate to the nearest pound, so that the budget can be agreed

questions.hint: It tests robustness.

questions.prompt: Which statement shows strong handling of uncertainty?

options.text: I would recommend the cheapest option because it carries the smallest risk if costs rise
My recommendation is correct on the figures given in the pack, and I would not change it
My recommendation holds unless demand falls below the level in the pack
It is impossible to know which option is best until more data is available to the team

questions.hint: It states the condition under which advice would change.

questions.prompt: Which action is reversible and so suited to acting on imperfect information?

options.text: Closing a service permanently
A small pilot in one region
Signing a ten-year contract
Selling a building

questions.hint: Pilots can be undone.

questions.prompt: What is a no-regrets action?

options.text: One that all stakeholders support, so that nobody has reason to regret it afterwards
One that has no costs attached, so that nothing is lost if the decision turns out to be wrong
One that is worth doing whichever scenario occurs
One that can be done within the existing budget, so that no new funding needs to be found

questions.hint: It pays off in every scenario.

questions.prompt: When might you defer an irreversible step?

options.text: Until a trigger point or further evidence makes it justified
Until the minister has approved it, because irreversible steps always need ministerial sign-off
Until the budget has been agreed for the following financial year and the funding is in place
For ever, because irreversible decisions should never be taken on the evidence available at the time

questions.hint: Waiting for a trigger reduces regret.

questions.prompt: Why consider who gains and loses from an option?

options.text: To decide which stakeholder to inform first, so that the loudest voices do not hear second-hand
To estimate the number of complaints that the department will receive after the decision
To check fairness and whether an equality impact assessment is needed
To choose the cheapest option, as the groups that lose out are usually the most costly

questions.hint: Fairness and legal duties.

questions.prompt: What should a recommendation say about monitoring?

options.text: That the project team will monitor progress and report to the board whenever there is a problem
That success will be reported in the annual report, which is where public bodies account for results
Which measures you would track, when you would review and what would make you change course
That monitoring will begin once the decision has been taken and the main activity is under way

questions.hint: It shows managing decisions.

questions.prompt: A candidate presents a single cost figure as certain. What is the weakness?

options.text: It ignores uncertainty and does not test the recommendation against changed assumptions
It omits the benefits of the option, which should be set against the cost in any comparison
A single figure cannot be used in a case study, because panels expect ranges for every number
It suggests the candidate has not read the pack closely, because every figure in the pack is a range

questions.hint: Honest ranges are better.

items.title: L13: In-tray items on information rights, gifts and the media
items.source: Freedom of Information Act 2000; UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 (ICO guidance); Civil Service Code (GOV.UK)
items.body:
In-tray exercises for senior roles often include items on information rights, hospitality and press enquiries. Knowing the basics lets you respond calmly and correctly.

Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, a public authority must normally respond to a valid request for information within 20 working days. A request must be in writing, give a name and an address for reply and describe the information sought. It does not have to mention the Act. An FOI request is not a reason to delay: log it, pass it to the information rights team promptly and note the deadline.

A subject access request under UK GDPR allows individuals to ask for their own personal data. The usual time limit is one month from receipt, and it may be extended in some circumstances. Again, the proper course is to forward it to the data protection team quickly instead of replying alone, because the department must check what it holds and protect other people's data.

Gifts and hospitality are governed by the Civil Service Code and departmental rules. Officials must not accept gifts or hospitality that might appear to influence their judgement, and should record and often declare those they are offered. A modest, routine item may be allowed under local rules, but an expensive gift from a supplier during a tender is not.

Press enquiries should usually go to the press office. Officials do not normally speak to the media on behalf of the department unless authorised, and they must not leak information. If a journalist contacts you directly, note the enquiry and refer it.

Where an item combines issues, such as a journalist's request that overlaps with an FOI, show that you spot both and route each to the right team.

questions.prompt: What is the usual time limit for a public authority to respond to a valid FOI request?

options.text: 40 calendar days
One month
10 working days
20 working days

questions.hint: The Freedom of Information Act 2000 sets 20 working days.

questions.prompt: Which of these must a valid FOI request include?

options.text: Payment of a standard fee, which the authority then refunds if the information is released
A reference to the Freedom of Information Act, so that the authority knows how to deal with it
A statement of the reason for the request, so that the authority can judge whether it is in the public interest
A name, an address for reply and a description of the information sought

questions.hint: These are the requirements for a valid request.

questions.prompt: An FOI request arrives in your in-tray. What is the right action?

options.text: Hold it until the end of the month and then deal with several requests together, so as to save time
Ask the requester why they want the information, so that you can decide whether to respond
Log it and pass it promptly to the information rights team, noting the deadline
Reply yourself with the information you think is relevant, since you know the subject best

questions.hint: Prompt routing protects the deadline.

questions.prompt: What is the usual time limit for responding to a subject access request?

options.text: One month from receipt
20 working days, as for every other information request that a public authority receives
Five working days, since individuals are entitled to see their own data without delay
Three months, because the information may be held in more than one system and take time to find

questions.hint: UK GDPR sets one month.

questions.prompt: Why should a subject access request go to the data protection team rather than be answered directly?

options.text: The department must check what it holds and protect other people's data
Individual officials are not allowed to see personal data, even where it is part of their own work
Only the data protection team can recognise the individual who is asking for their data
Requests must always be answered by a lawyer, because the response is a legal document

questions.hint: Careful handling.

questions.prompt: A supplier in the middle of a tender sends you an expensive gift. What should you do?

options.text: Share it among the team, so that nobody is seen to have gained personally from the offer
Decline or return it, and record the offer according to the rules
Accept it and keep it quiet, since a gift from a supplier is a private matter between two people
Accept it and declare it after the tender has been awarded, when it can no longer affect the decision

questions.hint: Gifts that might influence judgement should not be accepted.

questions.prompt: A journalist emails you directly asking about a policy. What is the usual correct response?

options.text: Ignore the email, because only the minister's office is allowed to respond to the media
Forward it to the minister's office and ask them to deal with it, without telling the press office
Answer informally and off the record, since that is the way that officials usually help journalists
Refer the enquiry to the press office and do not comment

questions.hint: Officials do not speak for the department without authority.

questions.prompt: Which statement about gifts and hospitality is correct?

options.text: The rules apply only to senior grades, since junior staff do not make decisions on public money
All small gifts can be accepted without any record, as they are too minor to influence anyone
Items that might appear to influence judgement should not be accepted, and offers are usually recorded
Gifts from suppliers are acceptable if you are not the person who makes the decision on the contract

questions.hint: The Code requires integrity.

questions.prompt: A journalist's request overlaps with an FOI request. What should you do?

options.text: Spot both, route the FOI to the information rights team and the press enquiry to the press office
Treat them as a single press enquiry and let the press office decide how to respond to both
Answer the journalist first, since press deadlines are shorter than the statutory limit for FOI
Combine them into one response that goes to the journalist and is also logged as the FOI reply

questions.hint: Show you recognise both.

questions.prompt: Which action would breach the Civil Service Code?

options.text: Declining a gift from a supplier, and recording that it was offered
Logging an FOI request on the day it arrives and passing it to the information rights team
Passing a draft policy paper to a journalist before it is announced
Referring a press call to the press office, even though the journalist asked you directly

questions.hint: Leaking breaches integrity.

items.title: L13: Tough and unexpected questions at HEO and SEO level
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Success Profiles (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Senior-grade interviews often include questions designed to test judgement rather than rehearsed material. Four types appear regularly.

The first is the disagreement question: 'Tell us about a time you disagreed with a decision.' A strong answer shows that you raised your concerns clearly and with evidence at the right time, listened to the reasons, and then supported the decision once it was taken, provided it was lawful and ethical. The Civil Service tradition is to challenge constructively and then commit. If you thought the decision was unlawful or improper, the Code sets out how to raise a concern, first with line management or the nominated officer, and if necessary with the Civil Service Commission.

The second is the prioritisation question: 'You have three urgent tasks and one hour.' Say how you would decide, perhaps by impact and deadline, whom you would tell and what you would drop or delegate.

The third is the 'first hundred days' question. A good answer is not a list of changes. It begins with listening and learning: understanding the team, the stakeholders and the delivery risks, agreeing priorities with your manager, and choosing one or two early visible improvements.

The fourth is the values question: 'What does impartiality mean to you in this job?' Give a practical example, such as providing the same quality of advice to ministers of different parties.

In all four, avoid stock phrases. If you need time, say so. If your answer includes a clear decision, the reason and the consequence, the panel has something to score.

Finally, keep to the question asked. A long answer that drifts risks losing the evidence the panel wanted.

questions.prompt: What does 'challenge constructively and then commit' mean?

options.text: Keep disagreeing until the decision is changed, since persistence shows how strongly you feel
Challenge only in private and never in front of others, so that the decision-maker is never embarrassed
Raise concerns clearly and with evidence at the right time, then support a lawful decision once taken
Stay silent until a decision is made, and then comply, since challenge is for ministers only

questions.hint: It balances challenge and support.

questions.prompt: Which answer to 'Tell us about a time you disagreed with a decision' is strongest?

options.text: I disagreed but said nothing, because it was not my place to question a decision taken above me
I disagreed, then told my team that the decision was mistaken so that they would understand the delays
I disagreed and kept raising it with each new manager until the decision was finally reversed
I raised my concerns with figures before the decision, listened to the reasons and then helped to deliver it

questions.hint: Constructive challenge followed by commitment.

questions.prompt: You think a decision is unlawful. What does the Code say you should do first?

options.text: Refuse to implement the decision
Tell the press
Raise it with the Civil Service Commission straight away
Raise it with line management or the nominated officer

questions.hint: Internal routes first.

questions.prompt: Asked to prioritise three urgent tasks in one hour, what should the answer include?

options.text: A statement that you cannot prioritise without more information about what each task involves
The order in which you would do the tasks, with no explanation, to keep the answer short
How you would decide, whom you would tell and what you would drop or delegate
A promise to complete all three tasks in the hour by working faster and cutting breaks

questions.hint: Reasoning and communication.

questions.prompt: Which approach to the 'first hundred days' question is strongest?

options.text: A list of the changes you would make in each area, to show that you have a clear plan
A statement that you would change nothing until you were confident, so that you cannot make a mistake
Listening and learning first, agreeing priorities and choosing one or two early improvements
A promise to restructure the team within the first month, so that the new direction is clear

questions.hint: It shows judgement and listening.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows impartiality?

options.text: Refusing to work on policies that are controversial, so that you remain neutral
Voting for no party at elections, so that nobody can say you favour any one of them
Giving the same quality of advice to ministers of different parties
Never discussing politics at work, in case a colleague thinks you hold a political view

questions.hint: Impartiality is acting equally for all governments.

questions.prompt: If you need a moment to think before answering a tough question, what should you do?

options.text: Say so and take a short pause
Ask the panel to move on
Start answering and work it out as you go
Repeat the question aloud several times

questions.hint: A pause is acceptable.

questions.prompt: A candidate answers the disagreement question by describing how a colleague was wrong. What is the weakness?

options.text: It does not mention a result, which is the only part that the panel marks
It uses a colleague's name, which breaches confidentiality whatever the circumstances
It focuses on blaming rather than what the candidate did and learned
It is too short to give evidence, because a disagreement needs a long account

questions.hint: The panel scores your actions.

questions.prompt: Why avoid stock phrases in tough questions?

options.text: They give the panel nothing specific to score
They are against the interview rules, which require candidates to use their own words
They take too long to deliver, so the panel runs out of time for later questions
They suggest you have prepared, and panels mark down any evidence of preparation

questions.hint: Specific evidence.

questions.prompt: Why keep to the question asked?

options.text: A drifting answer may lose the evidence the panel wanted
The chair has a time limit for each question, and unused time cannot be carried forward
The panel will cut you off, as the chair is told to stop any answer after three minutes
Long answers are penalised, because a longer answer is taken to show weaker judgement

questions.hint: Focus.

items.title: L13: Turning feedback into a plan and building promotion evidence
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Civil Service Learning guidance (GOV.UK)
items.body:
After one or more unsuccessful interviews, effective candidates turn feedback into a plan with a timescale. A plan that covers the next three months is realistic and keeps momentum.

Start by sorting feedback into types. Presentation issues, such as structure and pace, can be improved quickly through practice. Evidence issues, such as examples that are too small for the grade, take longer because you need new experiences. Knowledge issues, such as understanding how the department works, can be addressed through reading and conversations.

For each issue, set one specific action, a date and a way to know it has worked. 'Improve my answers' is too vague. 'Rewrite my three main examples to show my personal actions and one measured result, and test them on a colleague by the end of the month' is a plan.

Building evidence at the next level is the hardest part, and it needs support. Ask your line manager for stretch work, such as leading a small workstream, representing the team at a cross-department meeting or covering part of a manager's role. Temporary promotion, where available, often gives the strongest evidence for a substantive promotion. Shadowing, mentoring and sponsorship each help in different ways: a mentor offers advice and a sponsor with influence speaks for you when opportunities arise.

Keep a record of evidence as it happens, including the situation, your actions and the result, with dates, figures and written feedback from colleagues. Memory fades, and a log makes later applications easier.

Review progress with your manager, and share your goal so that they can help. Finally, choose when to try again. Reapplying quickly with the same evidence is rarely effective; reapplying when you have new evidence usually is.

questions.prompt: Feedback says your answers had poor structure and pace. How quickly can this usually be improved?

options.text: Not at all, because delivery style is a personal trait that panels do not expect to change
Quickly, through deliberate practice
Only over a year or more, since habits of speaking take a long time to change
Only through formal training provided by the department, since practice on its own does not work

questions.hint: Presentation issues respond to practice.

questions.prompt: Feedback says your examples were too small for the grade. Why does this take longer to fix?

options.text: You need to practise your delivery, as the examples will then sound bigger to the panel
You need to rewrite the examples, because the problem lies in how they were described, not what happened
You need to learn more about how the department works, so that the examples have more context
You need new experiences at a higher level

questions.hint: Evidence must be gained.

questions.prompt: Which is a specific action in a development plan?

options.text: Be more confident in the room, so that the panel can see the strength of my evidence
Improve my answers by the next interview, using the points that were raised in the feedback
Rewrite my three main examples to show personal actions and a measured result, and test them on a colleague by the end of the month
Do more interview practice over the next few months, with anyone who is willing to help

questions.hint: Specific, dated and testable.

questions.prompt: What can your line manager do to help you gain next-level evidence?

options.text: Offer stretch work such as leading a workstream or covering part of a manager's role
Tell you to apply for promotion, since the panel will give you feedback on any gaps
Move you to another team, so that you have a fresh start and are not defined by past interviews
Write a reference for your next application, which will carry more weight than new evidence

questions.hint: Stretch work gives evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is temporary promotion useful?

options.text: It often gives strong evidence of performing at the higher grade
It guarantees a substantive promotion when the period ends, provided your performance is good
It removes the need for any interview, because the department already knows your work
It increases your pay permanently, even after the temporary period has come to an end

questions.hint: It shows the level in practice.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a mentor and a sponsor?

options.text: A sponsor gives developmental feedback and a mentor does not, as a mentor is mainly a friend
They are the same role, and the two words are used interchangeably in the Civil Service
A mentor is always more senior than a sponsor, who is usually a peer outside the department
A mentor advises; a sponsor with influence speaks for you when opportunities arise

questions.hint: Different roles.

questions.prompt: Why keep a record of evidence as it happens?

options.text: It prevents disputes with managers about who did what, as the log is a binding record
HR requires a log, and it must be shared with the panel before the interview
It lets you share the log with panels, who will use it to check what you claim
Memory fades, and a log with dates, figures and feedback makes later applications easier

questions.hint: Contemporaneous notes help.

questions.prompt: Which is a sound time to reapply?

options.text: Whenever you feel ready, because confidence is the main thing the panel looks for
As soon as the next vacancy appears, since each interview gives you more practice
After about a year, whatever your progress, since panels expect a gap between applications
When you have new evidence at the level

questions.hint: New evidence changes the outcome.

questions.prompt: Why share your promotion goal with your manager?

options.text: So that they can look for a replacement in your current role without delay
So that they can help you find opportunities
So that they will promote you without needing to put you through a competition
So that they can write your application for you and present it to the panel

questions.hint: Managers can help.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of 'Improve my answers' as a plan?

options.text: It is too vague to act on or to show progress
It is too slow to be useful, as a plan should aim for results within a week
It is too ambitious for the time available, since improvement of that kind takes several years
It is too formal, because plans of this kind should not be written down

questions.hint: Plans need specifics.
